messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Pita was seventy-one when the world fractured for him, though the fracture itself occurred years prior at an outdoor gallery commission he had been painting. He had been mixing ochre and cadmium on his palette when the coordinated blast at the nearby transit hub sent a shockwave through the street. Brick dust coated his tongue, the deafening roar filled his ears, and he instinctively dropped to his knees, pressing his shoulders against the damp masonry wall to shield his head. He survived by holding his breath until his lungs burned, waiting for secondary explosions that never came. Now, the memories did not arrive as stories but as immediate intrusions that forced their way into his mind whenever the wind carried the faint scent of diesel or the glint of shattered glass. They were terribly clear and detailed, each flash replaying the exact weight of the rubble against his chest. As the weeks bled into months, Pita began to feel his body brace in that same defensive crouch whenever he stepped past his front door, his muscles locking as if he were still shielding himself from the fall. The relentless return of these vivid images slowly rewired his understanding of safety. He found himself certain that the world was a dangerous place, a conviction that settled in his chest like a cold stone. He could no longer trust his own judgment to keep him safe, nor could he rely on other people to look out for him. This growing sense of helplessness drove him to adopt rigid habits. He started calling his sister multiple times a day, asking her repeatedly to reassure him that he was okay and that the streets were secure. When the anxiety surged, he forced himself to swallow his fear, clamping his jaw and focusing intently on his breathing to maintain emotional control. He simply stopped going out, leaving his paint supplies to dry in the corners of his studio. Because he avoided stepping outside, his nervous system never had the chance to learn that the current was safe, and his attempts to clamp down on his feelings only left his nerves stretched and hyper-vigilant. The more he sought external validation and restrained his distress, the more isolated he felt, cementing his belief that he could not rely on himself or anyone else. Over the following year, these patterns coiled into a self-sustaining loop that left him exhausted. His refusal to go out meant the external world remained a theoretical threat, while his efforts to control his emotions kept his body braced for danger. Every time he called his sister for reassurance, the temporary relief only faded, leaving him more convinced that he could not rely on himself to navigate uncertainty. When the memories would suddenly force their way back into his awareness, their vivid detail and the familiar bodily reenactment validated his conviction that the world was inherently dangerous and that neither he nor others could be trusted to keep him safe. Each avoidance behavior and every attempt at emotional control only fed this certainty, making the next intrusion feel more inevitable. He stopped mixing colors, watching his half-finished canvases collect dust, and his single life narrowed to the dwindling patience of his sister’s phone calls. At seventy-one, Pita finally sought help not because the fear vanished, but because the weight of staying trapped had become heavier than the terror of facing the past. He came to the clinic hoping to reclaim his hands and his studio, terrified that he would spend his remaining years waiting for another explosion that might never come. He wanted to paint again, but he feared that stepping outside would once again prove that he was utterly incapable of protecting himself.
